## Annotation

~~Annotation~~ is the process of **going "back"** from the features measured in an untargeted metabolomics experiment to the corresponding metabolites.

### Challenges

1. Unknown metabolites
2. Poor standardization of chromatography (in particular LC)
3. Bioinformatic infrastructures (_databases,workflows, ..._)


## Annotation Levels

```{r out.width="\\linewidth", out.height="0.8\\textheight", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("../images/annotation_levels.png")
```


## The tools for the trade

In the case of MS based experiments, the process of annotation requires the interpretation of the ionization pattern of each molecule and the additional information which can be derived from chromatography and fragmentation experiments

1. Chemical expertise
2. Database of standards (in-house or on-line)
3. Fragmentation experiments
4. Molecular Networks
5. Chemoinformatics and predictive models


## Fragmentation Experiments

```{r out.width="\\linewidth", out.height="0.55\\textheight", fig.align="center"}

```

* Fragmentation patterns are sensitive to the chemical structure
* MS/MS can be matched with databases of standards

# In silico annotation

## Chemoinformatics and predictive models

When the compound is not in any spectral library, the MS/MS spectrum can be compared with *structures*, which are available for millions of compounds

```{r out.width="\\linewidth", out.height="0.62\\textheight", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("../images/scheme_insilico.pdf")
```

## SIRIUS: how it works

::: incremental
1. **Molecular formula**: from the isotope pattern and from a *fragmentation tree*, which explains the fragments as losses from the precursor
2. **CSI:FingerID**: a machine learning model predicts from the MS/MS spectrum the *molecular fingerprint* (presence/absence of substructures) and searches it in structure databases (PubChem, biological databases)
3. **CANOPUS**: predicts the compound class from the fingerprint, also when the structure is in no database
:::

::: {.box-key .fragment}
**SIRIUS 4:** \footnotesize Dührkop K. et al. (2019) Nature Methods 16, 299--302 \
CSI:FingerID: Dührkop K. et al. (2015) PNAS 112, 12580--12585 \
CANOPUS: Dührkop K. et al. (2021) Nature Biotechnology 39, 462--471

\weblink{https://bio.informatik.uni-jena.de/software/sirius/}{bio.informatik.uni-jena.de/software/sirius}
:::

## MetFrag: how it works

::: incremental
1. **Candidates**: all the structures in a database (PubChem, ChemSpider, ...) with the mass (or formula) of the precursor
2. **In silico fragmentation**: the bonds of each candidate are broken, producing all its possible fragments
3. **Scoring**: the candidates are ranked by how well their fragments explain the measured peaks
4. **Additional evidence** can be added to the score: retention time, number of references, similarity with library spectra
:::

::: {.box-key .fragment}
**MetFrag:** \footnotesize Wolf S. et al. (2010) BMC Bioinformatics 11, 148 \
MetFrag relaunched: Ruttkies C. et al. (2016) Journal of Cheminformatics 8, 3

\weblink{https://msbi.ipb-halle.de/MetFrag/}{msbi.ipb-halle.de/MetFrag}
:::

## In silico annotation: notes

::: incremental
- The result is a **ranked list of candidates**, not an identification
- The right answer is not always the first ... and it can be missing if the compound is not in the database
- Chemical and biological knowledge is still needed: is the candidate plausible in my samples?
:::

::: {.box-red .fragment}
⚠️ In silico annotations are *putative* (level 2--3): only a chemical standard gives the final confirmation
:::

# Molecular Networks

## Molecular Networks: the idea

::: incremental
- Molecules sharing part of their structure produce similar fragments
- MS/MS spectra can be compared two by two: the more fragments they share, the higher their similarity
:::

```{r out.width="\\linewidth", out.height="0.5\\textheight", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("../images/scheme_mn_similarity.pdf")
```

## From similarities to a network

```{r out.width="\\linewidth", out.height="0.6\\textheight", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("../images/scheme_mn_network.pdf")
```

::: fragment
Clusters are chemical families: one identified node helps to annotate its neighbours, even when they are not in any database
:::

## GNPS

### Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking
Web platform for molecular networking: public spectral libraries, classical and feature-based molecular networks, now in its second version (GNPS2)

\weblink{https://gnps2.org/}{gnps2.org}

### Reference
Wang M. et al. (2016) *Sharing and community curation of mass spectrometry data with Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking*. Nature Biotechnology 34, 828--837

## Feature-Based Molecular Networking

- The output of the preprocessing (`xcms`, MZmine, MS-DIAL) is exported to GNPS: the feature table and one MS/MS spectrum for each feature

::: fragment
- The nodes are the **features** of our data matrix:
    * isomers with different retention times are kept separate
    * nodes carry the intensities: the study design can be shown on the network (e.g. red vs white wines)
:::

::: {.box-key .fragment}
**Reference:** Nothias L.-F. et al. (2020) *Feature-based molecular networking in the GNPS analysis environment*. Nature Methods 17, 905--908
:::

## Molecular networks: our work

### Noise filtering in MS/MS spectra
Removing noise peaks increases the similarity of related spectra and gives networks with fewer false connections; with a data-driven choice of the threshold

Dalla Valle N. et al. (2025) Analytical Chemistry 97, 15873--15882

\weblink{https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.5c02109}{doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.5c02109}

### Neutral molecular networks
MS/MS spectra acquired in positive and negative ionization are merged in "neutral pseudo-spectra": one network, independent of the polarity

Dalla Valle N. et al. (2026) Analytica Chimica Acta 1415, 345708

\weblink{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2026.345708}{doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2026.345708}
